title: Adverse drug events associated with hydroxychloroquine: A real-world pharmacovigilance study from 2004 to 2024 using the FAERS database.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is an antimalarial and immunomodulatory drug widely used to treat autoimmune diseases and other conditions. Despite its significant efficacy, HCQ can cause adverse effects such as gastrointestinal issues, retinal toxicity, and cardiotoxicity. As the application of HCQ in immunotherapy expands, its safety and long-term effects need to be evaluated through big data and clinical observations. In a post-marketing surveillance study conducted from the first quarter of 2004 to the third quarter of 2024, we analyzed HCQ-related adverse event (AE) from the The FDA's Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, aiming to provide clinical references for its use.
METHODS: This retrospective pharmacovigilance study, based on the FAERS database, aimed to explore the association between HCQ and AEs. AE data from 2004 to 2024 were collected, with AE reports of the primary suspected drugs retrieved from the FAERS database. We filtered and analyzed reports related to HCQ use. Four different methods - reporting odds ratio, proportional reporting ratio, the multi-item gamma Poisson shrinker, and Bayesian confidence propagation neural network - were applied to perform disproportionality analysis on the AEs associated with HCQ.
RESULTS: The year 2020 had the highest number of AE reports, accounting for 20.44% of the total. In gender-based analysis, women were more likely to report AEs such as rheumatoid arthritis, disease exacerbation, drug intolerance, nausea, and pain, while men were more prone to report ECG QT prolongation and acute kidney injury. The study highlighted the differences in AE distribution across age groups and genders and pointed out that most AEs occurred within 1 month of starting HCQ; however, the risk of AEs remained even after 2 years, emphasizing the importance of long-term monitoring. The findings provided a reference for healthcare professionals and policymakers in developing safer drug usage guidelines.
CONCLUSION: This study emphasizes that HCQ-related adverse reactions are influenced by factors such as gender, age, and underlying diseases, revealing the potential risks associated with the widespread use of HCQ, particularly the risks related to severe adverse reactions. It underscores the importance of continuous drug safety monitoring and suggests the need for individualized risk assessments in clinical settings, especially for patients on long-term use or combination therapies.

title: Tropheryma Whipplei Infection Mimicking Sarcoidosis with an Atypical Course: A Molecularly Confirmed Diagnosis without PAS-Positive Intestinal Disease.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The bacterium Tropheryma whipplei causes Whipple's disease, a rare chronic infection that can involve virtually any organ, especially in the late phase, and mimic inflammatory or neoplastic conditions. The interval from first symptoms to diagnosis is typically several years.
CASE DESCRIPTION: A 68-year-old man was referred for pulmonary re-evaluation 2 years after a non-caseating hilar lymph-node granuloma had led to a diagnosis of stage I (nodal) sarcoidosis. His records revealed a 3-year history of lymphadenopathy with persistently elevated C-reactive protein and a two-year history of recurrent fever and fatigue. Corticosteroid therapy for ankle synovitis caused symptomatic worsening, prompting further investigation. Extensive infectious, oncological, rheumatological and tropical-medicine workup was unrevealing. Detailed history-taking revealed a 6 kg weight loss and epigastric discomfort, and a prior short antibiotic course for incipient pneumonia had produced transient improvement, making an atypical infectious aetiology, specifically Whipple's disease, plausible. An endobronchial ultrasound-guided lymph-node aspirate and subsequently a stool sample were both positive for T. whipplei by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), whereas cerebrospinal fluid PCR was negative, establishing systemic disease without central nervous system involvement. Oral doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine produced fast and sustained clinical and biochemical remission at 1 year. Surveillance duodenal histology was periodic acid-Schiff-negative and structured clinical follow-up was arranged.
CONCLUSION: Whipple's disease is a great mimicker, but a treatable one, and should be considered in cases of chronic inflammation without evidence of a pathogen in primary microbiological analysis and in cases of sarcoidosis with an atypical course, particularly if symptoms do not improve or worsen while on corticosteroids.
LEARNING POINTS: Consider Whipple's disease in any chronic, culture- and serology-negative systemic inflammatory syndrome, particularly when a diagnosis of "sarcoidosis" based on non-caseating granulomas fails to respond to, or clinically worsens under, corticosteroids, because immunosuppression can accelerate the infection.The diagnosis can be established by Tropheryma whipplei-specific quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) on tissue (here, an endobronchial ultrasound-guided lymph-node aspirate) and on non-invasive samples (typically stool, less frequently saliva), even when classic gastrointestinal symptoms and periodic acid-Schiff-positive duodenal histology are absent. Confirmation on a second specimen and cerebrospinal fluid testing to exclude central nervous system involvement should precede the prolonged antibiotic course.Untreated Whipple's disease is progressive and potentially fatal. Prolonged combination antibiotic therapy with structured follow-up is curative in most patients, and persistent stool-PCR positivity in an otherwise asymptomatic patient with normal duodenal histology may reflect residual deoxyribonucleic acid or colonisation rather than treatment failure.
journal: European journal of case reports in internal medicine

title: Chronic Calcific Pancreatitis as the Probable Initial Manifestation of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus With Mixed Connective Tissue Disease Overlap: A Case Report.
abstract: Chronic calcific pancreatitis as the presenting manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is exceedingly rare, particularly in tropical regions where it may be misattributed to tropical chronic pancreatitis (TCP). A 22-year-old Bangladeshi male farmer presented with a one-year history of recurrent postprandial epigastric pain and steatorrhea. Three months before admission, he developed inflammatory polyarthritis, a photosensitive malar rash, oral ulcers, Raynaud phenomenon, and progressive proximal muscle weakness. Investigations revealed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (50 × 109/L), a positive direct Coombs test, and a broad autoantibody profile including strongly positive antinuclear antibodies, anti-dsDNA, anti-U1-RNP, anti-nucleosome, anti-Ku, and anti-ribosomal P antibodies. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed chronic calcific pancreatitis with beaded main pancreatic duct dilatation (10-11 mm), diffuse intraductal calculi, and parenchymal atrophy, without features of autoimmune pancreatitis. He fulfilled the 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria for SLE (score 22) and the Sharp criteria for mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) overlap. Alcohol use, gallstone disease, hypercalcemia, hypertriglyceridemia, pancreatotoxic drugs, and cassava exposure were absent, but genetic testing and serum IgG4 were unavailable. Hydroxychloroquine, prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, and pancreatic enzyme replacement were followed by improvement of the systemic features, including platelet normalization. On the available evidence, the pancreatic disease is most plausibly an early manifestation of SLE-MCTD overlap, although a hereditary or tropical contribution cannot be formally excluded. This case expands the spectrum of SLE-associated pancreatic disease and underscores the need for systematic autoimmune evaluation in young patients from tropical regions with unexplained chronic calcific pancreatitis.

title: Isoallolithocholic acid attenuates acute liver allograft rejection by promoting Treg differentiation through the NR4A1/FOXP3 signaling axis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute allograft rejection driven by disordered CD4+ T cell alloimmunity severely limits long-term graft survival following orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT). Conventional broad-spectrum immunosuppressants cause severe systemic side effects, while therapeutic approaches relying on metabolites to induce transplant tolerance remain insufficiently explored. Isoallolithocholic acid (isoallo-LCA), a secondary bile acid produced by gut microbiota, maintains Treg homeostasis, yet its biological function and molecular mechanisms in regulating hepatic alloimmune rejection have not been clarified.
OBJECTIVE: To systematically explore the therapeutic efficacy of isoallo-LCA against acute liver allograft rejection and uncover its underlying molecular regulatory mechanism.
METHODS: An MHC-mismatched murine orthotopic liver transplantation acute rejection model was established. Recipient survival, liver pathological injury, BANFF rejection scores and serum hepatic injury indicators (ALT, AST, TBIL) were detected to evaluate the protective effect of isoallo-LCA. Flow cytometry was applied to analyze intrahepatic Th1 and Treg proportions. Transcriptomic sequencing combined with in vivo and in vitro western blot assays was used to screen and verify key signaling molecules, and an NR4A1 inhibitor was administered to conduct rescue validation experiments.
RESULTS: Isoallo-LCA intervention significantly prolonged recipient survival, alleviated intrahepatic inflammatory damage, lowered BANFF rejection grades and decreased serum ALT, AST and TBIL levels. Isoallo-LCA inhibited the differentiation of pro-inflammatory T-bet+ Th1 cells and promoted the expansion of FOXP3+ Tregs, restoring the balance of intrahepatic CD4+ T cell subsets. NR4A1 was identified as the core downstream effector of isoallo-LCA. Blockade of NR4A1 pharmacologically nearly eliminated the protective phenotypes mediated by isoallo-LCA, confirming the essential role of the NR4A1/FOXP3 signaling pathway.
CONCLUSION: Isoallo-LCA relieves acute liver allograft rejection by activating the NR4A1/FOXP3 signaling axis to remodel intrahepatic Th1/Treg immune balance. These findings provide preclinical evidence supporting gut microbial bile acid metabolites as potential low-toxic adjuvant candidates for inducing transplant immune tolerance, although clinical translation requires further validation in human studies.

title: Macrophage-specific TRAF6 deletion mitigates DSS-induced colitis and is associated with reduced Enterococcus abundance and altered arachidonic acid metabolism.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) involves dysregulated host immunity, gut microbial dysbiosis, and metabolic disturbances. As key innate immune cells, macrophages play critical roles in inflammatory responses, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and host-microbiota interactions. Tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6) is a key adaptor protein in pro-inflammatory signaling, but the role of macrophage TRAF6 in colitis-associated microbial and metabolic alterations remains unclear. Here, we used macrophage-specific Traf6 conditional knockout mice in a 3% DSS-induced colitis model. TRAF6 expression was increased in colonic tissues from DSS-treated mice and patients with IBD, with enhanced co-localization with CD68-positive macrophages. Macrophage-specific Traf6 deletion reduced colitis severity, inflammatory responses, and epithelial barrier injury. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed substantial gut microbiota remodeling, including reduced Enterococcus abundance. Untargeted metabolomics identified alterations in arachidonic acid metabolism: prostaglandin A2 (PGA2) was significantly reduced in both fecal and serum samples, whereas 12(S)-hydroxy-5Z,8E,10E-heptadecatrienoic acid [12(S)-HHT] was significantly reduced in feces and showed a similar downward trend in serum. Enterococcus abundance was positively associated with PGA2 and 12(S)-HHT levels, and an independent human IBD cohort further showed enrichment of Enterococcus. Collectively, macrophage-specific Traf6 deletion ameliorated DSS-induced colitis and was associated with coordinated remodeling of the gut microbiota and host metabolism, supporting an association between macrophage TRAF6, reduced Enterococcus abundance, and altered arachidonic acid metabolism during intestinal inflammation.
